finding: This round replaced §2's withdrawn sink-validation mechanism with a precondition I cannot satisfy inside this release, while the same section still ships the behaviour the precondition gates. §2 now states: "before `blocking` may gate, the severity a row carries must be checkable by something other than the row's author, and the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition", and then says the section "picks none" of the four answers to the second half. The only checker §2 offers for the first half is prose: severity "is checkable against the finding's own text by a later round" -- a later agent, not an artifact, so nothing in a task's acceptance can assert it. The one mechanical checker that was on the table is now fenced out by the tightened Non-Goal 3: "Any future proposal that makes `--record` refuse a row is a different release, and this one must gate on what is already recorded or not gate at all." Meanwhile §2's Default paragraph ships `blocking`, and §7 test 1 pins default `blocking` as acceptance. So the release simultaneously forbids `blocking` from gating until a condition is met, forecloses the only stated way to meet it, and requires a test asserting `blocking` is the default. Building this means picking one of the three by myself, and each pick changes what ships.
suggestion: Resolve the precondition against the default in one clause. Either (a) ship `all` as the default for this release and state that `blocking` becomes the default once the checkability requirement is discharged in a named later release, so §7 test 1 pins `all`; or (b) drop the word precondition -- state that `blocking` gates on the severity as recorded, with the self-declared-label risk accepted and named, and delete "before `blocking` may gate"; or (c) keep the precondition and name the artifact that discharges it inside this release, with a §7 test. Whichever is chosen, say explicitly whether the 67 recorded rows block `blocking` from being usable on this repository today.

finding: The requirement added this round uses the word "disposition" for something other than the `disposition` §3 defines two sections later, and the two readings produce opposite code. §2: "the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition" -- in context this means a decision about what to do with out-of-enum severities (migrate, ignore, treat as blocking, treat as advisory). §3: "A row carrying a `wontfix` or `duplicate` disposition is excluded from the round's finding count", i.e. a per-row stored key with a fixed vocabulary and an exclusion rule. An implementer decomposing §2 can discharge its requirement literally -- stamp a disposition on those 67 rows -- which under §3's rule silently excludes fifteen rounds of recorded findings from every count that reads them, and would look like compliance with both sections. Nothing in either section says the two words are different things.
suggestion: Use a different noun in §2 -- "a stated policy" or "a recorded decision" -- and add one clause naming what that decision ranges over (the four incompatible answers, even unchosen, are the range). If §3's `disposition` key is genuinely one of the candidate answers for the 67 rows, say so explicitly and say what it would mean; if it is not, say that stamping §3 dispositions on historical rows is not the migration.

finding: The `--check` requirement this round took back from `spec/0.46.0.md` §8 arrives as one sentence and nothing else, and that sentence makes a false statement about this document. §2.0a: "**It takes it back:** `--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`, and §7 gains the test that pins them equal." §7 holds eight tests and none of them names `--check`, `--status`, or a parity assertion -- tests 1-4 are the field and the replay, 5 is the disposition, 6-8 are the reset. So the section that adds the requirement asserts its own acceptance exists when it does not. Three further pieces I would have to invent to build it: (1) placement -- `converged` on both surfaces comes from `engine.Converged(rounds, required, hash)` (`audit_record.go:95` for --record, `:333` for --status/--check), which folds the streak internally, so "reads the same predicate" needs a statement of where the severity predicate enters that fold; (2) exit code -- `--status --check` is an exit-code gate, and the release never says what it exits when `blocking` is satisfied but non-blocking rows survive; (3) the surfacing half -- §2.0a itself records that `nonblocking_open` is review-only and that surfacing the remaining rows "means creating an audit-side counterpart, which this release must declare and test rather than assume -- §7 does not", and taking the requirement back did not add that declaration. §5 compounds this: it still lists "the `--check` divergence" among the three sections exported to `spec/0.46.0.md` and closes "This release is §2, §3 and §4", so a decomposer reading §5 will not create a `--check` task at all.
suggestion: Add the §7 test the sentence claims -- e.g. "a state in which `--record` counts a round clean under `blocking` is reported converged by `--status --check` at the same audit_clean_rounds, and the two disagree under `all`" -- and state its exit code. Name the audit-side counterpart to `nonblocking_open` (key, value, which surfaces carry it) or say plainly that surviving non-blocking rows are surfaced by an existing key. Amend §5 so the `--check` half is no longer listed as exported, or the takeback and the removal notice will decompose into different releases.

finding: §4 now picks an implementation site -- "the reset is applied by the audit caller ... The audit-caller form is the one that composes" -- and that pick cannot reach the value the release gates on. The two call sites §4 cites (`audit_record.go:101`, `:339`) are the two places `consecutive_clean` is printed. The value that decides anything is `converged`, and it is not computed from those calls: `engine.Converged(rounds, requiredCleanRounds, currentHash)` (`engine/reviewstate.go:510`) calls `ConsecutiveClean` inside itself, and audit reaches it at `audit_record.go:95` (--record) and `audit_record.go:333` (--status/--check), with `cli/run_status.go:149` and `cli/budget.go:26` reading it for the run driver and the budget signal. An audit caller cannot make that fold hash-aware without a new engine entry point, and §4 names none; Non-Goal 4 forbids changing the shared one because `review_status.go:67` calls the same function. Built as §4 now specifies it, the reset changes two printed integers while `converged`, `budget_exhausted`, `tp resume` and `tp run`'s oracle keep the pre-reset answer -- and §2.0a in this same round made `--check`, which reads exactly that `converged`, a requirement of this release. §4 also states the collision only against `review_status.go:91`, which is the printed integer, not `:67`, which is the predicate.
suggestion: Name the function this release adds -- e.g. `engine.AuditConsecutiveClean(rounds)` (hash-aware trailing walk) and `engine.AuditConverged(rounds, required, currentHash)` -- and list every audit call site that must switch to them: `audit_record.go:95`, `:101`, `:333`, `:339`, `audit.go:352`, plus the audit branches of `run_status.go:149` and `budget.go:26`. State that `engine.ConsecutiveClean` and `engine.Converged` keep their current semantics for review, which is the form that actually satisfies Non-Goal 4. Then add a §7 test asserting `converged`, not just `consecutive_clean`, changes across a spec_hash boundary.

finding: "Retroactive over rounds already on disk" is new in §4 this round and is offered only as a benefit ("makes §7 test 7 true by construction rather than by fixture"). Its cost is unstated and it is not hypothetical on this repository: measured from `spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json`, that cycle's nine audit rounds are clean only at r8 (`sha256:1259a4a`) and r9 (`sha256:54e031e`) -- the hash moved between the only two clean rounds. With `audit_clean_rounds: 2` (`.tp/config.json`), the hash-aware trailing walk stops at that boundary, so `consecutive_clean` falls from 2 to 1 and `engine.Converged` turns false for a cycle that is recorded as converged and shipped. An operator who installs this release changes the answer `tp audit spec/0.35.0.md --status --check` gives about work that is finished, on no new evidence, with no round recorded. §7 covers only the other direction: test 8 asserts a cycle whose spec never changed keeps its streak, and neither of this repository's two recorded audit cycles is such a cycle. The release states no migration, no version gate, no grace for rounds recorded before the rule existed, and nothing about what `tp resume` or `tp run` should do when a previously-released phase reopens.
suggestion: State the upgrade behaviour explicitly and choose one: apply the walk only to rounds recorded at or after this release (which needs a per-round marker, so say which field), or apply it retroactively and say so as a documented consequence with the remedy an operator has (record one more clean round, or `--reconcile` per `spec/0.45.0.md` §3). Add a §7 test over a fixture whose clean streak spans a hash change, asserting the converged value both before and after the rule. If the retroactive form is kept, `spec/0.35.0.md` and `spec/0.36.0.md` are the worked examples and belong in the release notes.

finding: Both paragraphs added to §3 this round describe defects in shipped code accurately and mandate nothing, so neither can be decomposed. The second is the sharper case: "`dedupAuditRows` (`audit_merge.go:191-203`) keys on `role\x00item_id` and keeps the **first** row, comparing nothing -- where review's merge keeps the highest severity. Under `blocking`, the order the role files are passed to `--merge` decides whether a round is clean." I verified the code claim -- lines 191-203 are exactly that loop and the doc comment says "keeping the first occurrence". But the spec states no required behaviour (keep the highest severity? refuse duplicate inputs? make the order canonical?), §7 has no test for it, and §6 does not fence it out as a Non-Goal. Since `blocking` is what makes the tiebreak gate-deciding, this is a defect the release creates and then leaves unassigned: the release ships correctly by every stated acceptance while the gate stays order-dependent. The first added paragraph has the same shape -- it ends "this release has to pick one" between live recomputation and carrying the disposition forward, and the section picks neither, which is the same absence one section earlier. The pattern to check across the spec: a round-N finding answered by pasting its measurement into the normative text instead of by adding a requirement or a Non-Goal.
suggestion: For the merge defect, add one normative sentence and a §7 test: e.g. "`dedupAuditRows` keeps the row with the blocking severity when two rows share `(role, item_id)`, matching review's merge", tested with the same two rows supplied in both orders and asserting an identical clean verdict. For the record-time/live-recompute paragraph, pick the form and state it, since §7 test 5 asserts different things under each. Generally: when a measured defect is recorded in a section, follow it with either the requirement it implies or a Non-Goal naming the release that takes it.

finding: Two conclusions I formed this round and discarded before recording them. (1) I had drafted a finding that §4's new derived-walk paragraph cites only `audit_record.go:101` and `:339` and therefore omits `audit.go:352`, so the prompt-framing streak would keep the pre-reset value -- the wrong conclusion being "this call site is unreported". Checking `review-round-2.ndjson` first, round 2's `reset-of-a-derived-value` already enumerates `audit.go:352` and `resume.go:87`, so the omission is on record and re-reporting it would have been a duplicate. What survived the check is narrower and is a consequence of the form §4 newly chose rather than of its citation list: the audit-caller form cannot reach `engine.Converged` at all, which is the row I did record. (2) I had concluded that §2's opening sentence -- "it is the reason the sink validation above is a precondition rather than a nicety" -- became a new defect this round because the sink validation it points at was withdrawn, so the reference now resolves to nothing rather than merely pointing the wrong way. Round 2 already carries `stale-directional-reference` and `directional-cross-reference-wrong` on that exact sentence, both unresolved, so the wrong conclusion would have been that a withdrawal turns an already-reported dangling reference into a new one.
suggestion: No action beyond the rows actually recorded. The generalisable habit: when a repair adopts a previous round's suggested mechanism, check whether the new finding is about the mechanism now chosen or about the defect that motivated it -- only the first is new.
